2 tablespoons fine salt, for the soaking water
2 tins diced tomatoes, about 800 g each
900 g kale or chard, stemmed and chopped
150 g grated parmesan, for the table
125 ml good olive oil, for drizzling

method: Soak the beans overnight in the water with the salt. Salted soaking water gives beans that cook more evenly with skins that stay intact, which is the opposite of the old advice and is what actually happens. Drain them before cooking.

Brown the sausage in your largest pot in four batches, not one. This is the step that does not scale: a crowded pot steams the meat grey and you lose the browning that carries the whole soup. Each batch wants a hot pan and space. Ground meat has to reach an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C), so check the thickest crumbles with an instant-read thermometer rather than judging by colour. Lift each batch out and keep the fat.

Cook the onion, carrot and celery in the sausage fat and olive oil until softened and browning at the edges. At this volume expect twenty to twenty-five minutes rather than the ten a small pot takes, and stir often so the bottom does not scorch.
Add the garlic, fennel seed and pepper flakes and cook until fragrant, then the tomato paste, cooking until it darkens to brick.
Add the drained beans, tomatoes, stock, bay leaves and parmesan rinds. Return the sausage. Bring to a boil, then hold it at a low simmer.

Simmer for about ninety minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom every twenty minutes. Beans sink and a twelve litre pot scorches easily. The soup is ready when a bean crushes smoothly against the roof of your mouth with no chalk at the centre — test five, since one soft bean proves nothing.
Add the greens and cook until they are tender and dark, five to ten minutes for kale and one or two for chard.

Now season, off the heat, in stages. Add half the salt, stir thoroughly, wait two minutes and taste. A pot this size takes several minutes to distribute salt, and tasting too soon leads to over-salting. Add the vinegar at the end.

Cooling is the part people get wrong. A full pot left on the stove stays in the temperature range where bacteria multiply for hours. Divide it into shallow containers no more than 8 cm deep, or set the pot in a sink of ice water and stir it down, and get it cold within a couple of hours.
To serve on the second day, reheat only what you need, bringing each batch to a full steaming simmer. Serve with parmesan, olive oil and bread.
notes: Feeding twenty-four: plan 500 ml a head for a working crew and 350 ml for a mixed room. Add a loaf of bread per six people and it stretches further than the numbers suggest.
What does not scale: browning, seasoning, and cooling. Everything else multiplies cleanly. Budget more time than the arithmetic suggests for the first and taste your way through the second.
Meatless version: leave out the sausage, double the fennel seed, add 700 g of mushrooms browned hard, and use vegetable stock. It is a good soup and it needs more salt than the meat version.
storage: Five days cold in shallow containers, and better on the second day. It freezes for four months and portions well into 1 litre containers. The greens go slack in the freezer, so if you plan to freeze most of the pot, add the greens by the batch when reheating instead.

title: The Last of Everything
dek: Friday soup, made from what is left. There is a structure to it, and it is not throwing things in a pot.
yield: About 3 litres, varies with what you have
intro: The end-of-week soup is the oldest thing in any kitchen, and it goes wrong when it becomes an act of disposal rather than of cooking. What separates a good one from a sad one is structure. Every soup that works has the same five parts: fat and aromatics browned at the start, a liquid with some body, a starch, something with texture added near the end, and acid plus salt to finish. If what you have covers those five, you have a soup. If it does not, you are missing a part and you should find it rather than adding more of what you already have.

items: 3 tablespoons fat — butter, olive oil, bacon fat or drippings
500 g aromatics — onion, leek, carrot, celery, garlic, in any proportion
2 litres liquid — stock, the water from cooking beans, or a tin of tomatoes plus water
400 g starch — potato, rice, pasta, barley, or cooked beans
400 g the rest — cooked meat, roasted vegetables, greens, corn, whatever is left
2 tablespoons acid — vinegar, lemon, or a spoon of pickle brine
2 teaspoons fine salt, and more to taste

ingredients.group: Things that rescue a dull pot
items: 1 tablespoon soy sauce or fish sauce
3 tablespoons chopped fresh herbs, any kind

method: Take stock of what you actually have before you turn on the heat, and sort it into the five parts. This takes two minutes and prevents the most common failure, which is a pot with three kinds of starch in it and nothing else.

Heat the fat in a heavy pot over medium-high and cook the aromatics with a pinch of salt until they are soft and browning at the edges, ten to twelve minutes. This is not the step to rush, whatever the rest of the ingredients are. Everything after this is assembly.

If you have tomato paste, add it now and cook until it turns brick coloured and smells sweet. If you have a spice you want to use, add it here too and cook it in the fat for thirty seconds until it smells toasted, rather than adding it to liquid later.

Add the liquid, scraping the pot bottom until nothing is stuck. Drop in a parmesan rind if you have one, plus a bay leaf. Simmer for ten minutes to give it a chance to become one thing rather than several.

Add the starch and cook until it is tender — twenty minutes for raw potato or barley, ten for rice, two for cooked beans or leftover pasta. If you want leftovers of the leftovers, cook the pasta or rice separately and add it by the bowl, since it will keep absorbing liquid overnight.

Add whatever else you have, in order of how long it needs. Roasted vegetables and cooked meat want three or four minutes to warm through. Hardy greens want five. Spinach wants one. Anything already cooked is being reheated, not cooked — if it goes in early it turns to mush.

Bring the pot to a full steaming simmer once everything is in. Leftovers being reheated should get to at least 165°F (74°C) throughout, which in practice means visibly steaming and bubbling rather than merely hot, and it is worth checking with an instant-read thermometer if there is cooked meat in there.

Now fix it. Taste. If it tastes thin, it needs salt. If it tastes flat and heavy after enough salt, it needs acid. If it tastes like nothing at all, it needs a savoury hit — soy sauce, a rind, a spoon of miso. Add one thing at a time and taste between them.
Finish with herbs, black pepper and a hard drizzle of olive oil. The oil at the end is not decoration; a soup made from leftovers is usually short on fat, and fat is what carries flavour.
notes: Things that do not belong: anything breaded, anything already sauced with a dairy sauce, cured olives in quantity, and more than one strongly flavoured leftover at a time. Two competing dinners in one pot taste like neither.

The freezer bag of vegetable ends, the bag of parmesan rinds and the container of bean cooking liquid are all worth keeping specifically for this. They cost nothing and they are exactly the parts that a leftovers soup is usually short of.
Blending is a legitimate rescue. A pot that looks like an accident becomes a respectable puree with an immersion blender and a swirl of cream, and nobody needs to know what was in it.
storage: Three days cold, which is shorter than the other soups here because the ingredients already had a life before this. Do not freeze it unless every component went in fresh — most of this pot has already been cooled and reheated once, and each round costs texture. If in doubt about how long something has been in the cold, it goes in the bin rather than the pot.
